content: The implementation of national action plans to combat antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a critical responsibility of health ministries. This document is particularly relevant for personnel working in health ministries, health service departments, and those overseeing health facility accreditation, regulation, healthcare quality improvement, public health, disease control, water and sanitation, occupational health, and antimicrobial stewardship programs. At the facility level, the primary audience includes administrators of acute healthcare facilities, such as chief executive officers, who are tasked with similar responsibilities. The core components outlined in this document are designed to support the implementation of infection prevention and control (IPC) programs at both national and local levels. These components are particularly relevant to IPC leaders, safety and quality managers, local teams, and regulatory bodies. While the recommendations focus on acute healthcare facilities, the expert panel emphasizes that the principles and practices of IPC to prevent healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) are universally applicable to any healthcare setting. Therefore, these guidelines should also be adapted for use in community, primary care, and long-term care facilities as they develop and review their IPC programs. Organizations such as academic institutions, national IPC professional bodies, non-governmental organizations involved in IPC activities, and civil society groups may also find these core components valuable. Given the close relationship between water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) and IPC, the document is additionally relevant to WASH leaders at both national and facility levels in all countries. Furthermore, the core components of IPC programs should be implemented not only in public healthcare systems but also in private healthcare facilities. The primary objective of these guidelines is to provide evidence-based and expert consensus recommendations on the essential components of IPC programs required at national and facility levels to prevent HAIs and combat AMR through effective IPC practices. These recommendations aim to offer a practical, effective, and acceptable framework for developing or strengthening IPC programs. They can be adapted to local contexts based on available resources and public health needs. The eight core components of IPC programs, initially published by the World Health Organization (WHO) in 2009, and the ten key components identified through the SIGHT review, served as the foundation for these recommendations. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) evaluated the relevance of these components alongside evidence from systematic reviews to develop the core components listed in these guidelines. Most of the new core components align with those previously identified. It is important to note that the numbered list of core components does not imply a ranking of their importance; all components are equally critical for establishing and maintaining effective IPC programs. As countries and facilities implement these core components or review and strengthen their existing IPC programs, they may prioritize specific components based on their context, previous achievements, and identified gaps. The long-term goal is to build a comprehensive approach encompassing all eight core components. The guidelines emphasize that IPC implementation is integral to strengthening health systems. The availability of guidelines defining the core components of IPC programs enhances the capacity of member states to develop and implement effective technical and behavior-modifying interventions. These interventions directly impact the burden of HAIs and AMR, including outbreaks of highly transmissible diseases, where the effectiveness of implementation can be rapidly observed. Access to healthcare services designed to minimize the risk of avoidable HAIs for patients and healthcare workers is a fundamental human right. Effective and integrated IPC is a public health priority and significantly contributes to strengthening core capacities and health service resilience within the framework of the International Health Regulations (IHR). The prevention and control of HAIs also play a vital role in achieving the United Nations' health-related Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Furthermore, effective IPC is a key determinant of healthcare quality, essential for achieving people-centered, integrated universal health coverage. The development of these guidelines followed the WHO Handbook for Guideline Development and included six main stages: identifying primary outcomes and formulating research questions, conducting systematic reviews, developing an inventory of national and regional IPC action plans, assessing and synthesizing evidence, formulating recommendations and good practice statements, and writing the guidelines with dissemination and implementation strategies. The process involved contributions from four main groups: the WHO Guideline Steering Group, the Guideline Development Group (GDG), the External Peer Review Group, and systematic review teams. The WHO Guideline Steering Group, chaired by the Director of the Department of Service Delivery and Safety, played a central role in drafting the initial scope, identifying critical outcomes, and formulating research questions. The GDG, comprising 27 external experts and stakeholders from diverse professional backgrounds and geographical regions, appraised the evidence, formulated recommendations, and reviewed the final guideline document. The External Peer Review Group, consisting of six technical experts, reviewed the final document for accuracy, technical content, and contextual relevance. The systematic reviews conducted for these guidelines evaluated the effectiveness of key IPC components at both facility and national levels. The evidence was assessed using standardized methodologies, including the EPOC risk of bias criteria, and the quality of studies was graded as high, moderate, low, or very low. Recommendations were formulated based on the quality of evidence, the balance of benefits and harms, values and preferences, resource implications, and feasibility. The strength of recommendations was rated as either strong or conditional. In cases where direct evidence was lacking, the GDG developed good practice statements to highlight essential IPC components supported by indirect evidence. These statements emphasize actions deemed critical for IPC implementation. The guidelines also identify areas requiring further research to address gaps in evidence. Overall, these guidelines provide a comprehensive framework for implementing effective IPC programs at national and facility levels, aiming to reduce HAIs and combat AMR while promoting healthcare quality and resilience.
